newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish govt not considering property tax at present.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt not considering property tax at present.

text.p: Irish finance minister Ruairi Quinn said on Monday that the government was not considering any proposals relating to the residential property tax (RPT) at present.
"There are no proposals of any kind before the government at the present time in relation to RPT or local service charges," Quinn told Irish state radio.
Quinn's comments followed an Irish Times report that the property tax was likely to be abolished next year in a move linked to a major overhaul of local government funding.
The tax, which raises around 12 million Irish pounds annually, applies to property worth more than 101,000 punts and where the combined household income exceeds 30,100.
It has caused a lot of controversy since its introduction with critics arguing that it is inequitable and anti-urban.

Dublin residents in particular believe that they are unfairly penalised because of the higher price of property in the capital. Official figures show that Dublin residents paid 77 percent of the RPT take in 1995.
Quinn said the minister for the environment, Brendan Howlin, was conducting a study into how local government should be funded but the conclusions of the study had not yet come before the cabinet.
Asked about his tax plans in the next budget, Quinn said he would approach the next budget with the same degree of prudence as he had his previous two budgets.
He said taxes had been reduced in his last budgets and he hoped to be able to do that again but cautioned: "I am not going to risk the future of this economy just to be popular."
